title: Minestrone
subtitle: Italian vegetable and bean soup with pasta
excerpt: Minestrone is a thick Italian vegetable soup made with whatever vegetables are in season, always including beans, and usually finished with short pasta. The version here is a year-round recipe using tinned beans and a core set of vegetables, with parmesan rind added during cooking to enrich the broth.
sourceNotes: Minestrone is a broad Italian category rather than a fixed recipe. The name derives from the Italian 'minestra' (soup) and the suffix '-one' (big), indicating a large, substantial soup. It appears in Italian cooking texts from the 18th century onwards and varies significantly by region and season. The Milanese version uses arborio rice; the Genoese version contains pesto; the Roman version adds pasta. The version here follows the widespread northern Italian model.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the pasta. Add freshly cooked pasta when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: A large-batch soup by nature. Doubles well and keeps for 4 days in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the base a day ahead without the pasta. Add the pasta when reheating so it does not go soft.

content.text: Minestrone is a thick vegetable and bean soup with pasta. There is no single recipe: the vegetables change by season and region, and every Italian cook has their own version. The core elements are a soffritto base (onion, carrot, celery), beans, green vegetables, tomato, and some kind of pasta or rice to make it filling. A parmesan rind cooked in the soup adds depth and a slight creaminess to the broth.

items.prepNote: ditalini, small tubetti, or similar small pasta
about 5 cm, optional but worth it

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, celery, and garlic. Cook for 12 minutes until soft.
Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes. Add the potatoes, courgette, beans, stock, parmesan rind if using, and salt.
Bring to a simmer and cook for 35 to 40 minutes until the potatoes and courgette are very tender and the soup has thickened. Remove the parmesan rind.
Add the pasta and cook for the time indicated on the packet, stirring occasionally. The soup should be thick; add a splash of water if it is too stiff. Taste and adjust the salt.
Serve with a drizzle of olive oil and grated parmesan at the table.

Minestrone is made all over Italy, and each region and season produces a different version. In Milan, it is often made with arborio rice instead of pasta. In Genoa, a spoonful of pesto is stirred in at the end. In Rome, it is made with short pasta and a great deal of parmesan. The only things that stay constant across all versions are a soffritto base, beans, and the principle that the soup should be thick enough to support a spoon standing up in it.
